newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Q3 earnings up smartly, beat expectations.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Q3 earnings up smartly, beat expectations.

text.p: With the quarterly flood of U.S. corporate earnings not yet at the half-way point, the year-over-year earnings gains are solid and, more importanty, the numbers are beating Wall Street expectations.
But analysts are also saying earnings gains in 1997 are likely to be less robust than in 1996.

As for beating expectations, Chuck Hill, director of research at First Call, notes that estimates start out high early in the quarter only to be revised lower so that the target is easier to hit when the actual earnings come out.

Sam Stovall, director of industry information at Standard & Poor's Corp, said analysts at the firm freeze their earnings numbers at the end of the quarter and make no further revisions. He said the bigger companies are mostly meeting expectations -- but not reporting gains widely in excess of the mark.
"On a year-to-year basis earnings are looking very good," Stovall added.
"This will be the 14th quarter in a row that earnings on balance were better-than-expected," said Hugh Johnson, market strategist at First Albany Co.

Johnson noted that the current round has seen positive earnings surprises from some high profile companies widely followed on Wall Street. He cited Caterpillar Inc ; automakers General Motors Corp, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp ; Sears, Roebuck and Co and Merck and Co Inc.
Allstate Corp rose 3-1/2 to 54-7/8 Thursday after reporting better-than expected earnings of $0.58 per share.
"My guess is that this will continue next week," Johnson said. International Business Machines Corp is due to kick off next week's earnings torrent on Monday morning.

According to First Call's data, with about one-third of the companies in the Standard & Poor's 500 already reporting earnings, 27 percent have been five percent or more above the mean expectation; 51 percent have been at the mean to up five percent; 10 percent have been beneath expectations by no more than five percent; and 12 percent have been more than five percent worse than expected.
With 175 S&P companies reporting, the aggregate report is 4.2 percent over the expectation.
Hill said the the performance so far is a little better than the norm seen over the last two-and-one-half years.

Hill said that of about 5,000 companies in the First Call system, about 400 typically make "pre-announcements" that upcoming earnings will be at or close to a certain number. Of these, 60 percent are a warning that earnings will be lower than expected, and 40 percent of the time the companies say earnings will be at or above the expectation.

With the Dow industrials above the 6000 level, a key question is whether the generally good earnings support lofty valuations. One phenomenon, Johnson noted, is that better-than-expected numbers for the third quarter are causing analysts to make upward revisions to their estimates for 1997.

"The market is riding upward revisions in estimates of 1997 earnings for some companies," Johnson said. But he also noted exceptions. Texas Instruments Inc beat estimates by $0.03 per share, but 1997 estimates have come down. After grocery chain Albertson's Inc said estimates for its third and fourth quarters were too high, 1997 estimates have fallen from the $2.09 per share area to $2.02.

Stovall noted S&P economists expect earnings in 1997 to grow only three percent while the firm's industry analysts expect 13 percent growth. But he said he ie "cautiously optimistic" about the outlook for U.S. stocks.
